analysis.one_liner: Ends the tax deduction for bonuses over $1 million paid to all employees of public companies.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or any action on the House floor, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current tax law, publicly traded companies can deduct up to $1 million per executive in pay as a business expense, but pay above that line is only shielded from this rule for the top officers. This bill would extend the $1 million no-deduction rule to every employee of a publicly traded company, so no bonus above $1 million could be written off as a business cost. It would also cover companies that stopped filing public reports only within the last three years, and let the Treasury write rules to stop companies from dodging the limit by routing pay through other entities. It would take effect for tax years after 2020.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit indirectly: when corporations can no longer deduct multimillion-dollar bonuses as a business expense, those high earners and their companies pay more of the tax burden, which eases the load on everyone else. The bill's sponsors presented it as ending a federal subsidy for outsized executive pay.

how_it_helps.text: Current law already denies publicly traded corporations a deduction for each executive's pay above $1 million, but that limit applies only to top officers; this bill extends the denial to pay above $1 million for all employees of publicly traded corporations.

The bill reaches executives who left the top-officer ranks before 2021 by covering principal executive and financial officers and the three highest-paid officers for tax years back to 2016, so high earners cannot escape the limit by changing titles.

The bill closes an escape hatch by letting the Treasury write rules covering pay routed through pass-through or other entities to avoid the limit, and by covering companies that stopped filing public reports only within the past three years.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded corporations and their highest-paid employees. Any portion of an employee's compensation above $1 million would become a nondeductible expense, raising those companies' tax bills and the tax bills of their top earners.

drawbacks.text: The cap applies to all employees, not just executives, so it would also deny deductions for very large bonuses paid to non-executive staff, such as top salespeople or financial traders, which its critics said reaches beyond the 'corporate bonus' problem the bill's title targets.

Companies may respond by restructuring pay into forms not covered by the cap, which is why the bill gives the Treasury broad rule-writing authority; the need for such authority signals the limit could be avoided without close oversight.
The provisions looking back to tax years as early as 2016 reach past conduct, which taxpayers and their advisers generally oppose on grounds of fair notice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a fairness rule: businesses would no longer get a federal tax deduction for the portion of any employee's pay above $1 million, and the tax burden shifts from ordinary taxpayers toward highly compensated earners and their companies. The costs are limited and manageable: some non-executive employees with very large bonuses would be swept in, and companies would have an incentive to restructure pay, which the Treasury would have to police. On balance the bill addresses a targeted tax advantage for the highest earners at modest cost to companies.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on February 2, 2021, with 14 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
Sixteen Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor joined.
The Ways and Means Committee never held a markup or vote on the bill, and the full House never considered it; the bill's last action in Congress.gov is the February 2, 2021 committee referral.
The bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded corporations and their highest-paid employees are better off, because the tax deduction for pay above $1 million per person remains available. Ordinary taxpayers continue to bear a share of the cost of that deduction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public companies and their top earners

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 16 cosponsors.

for.name: 16 of 222 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress, leaving it dormant after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the committee chairman who let the bill sit was also a Democrat, so the divide ran within the majority party rather than between the parties.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations and their highest-paid employees
industries.note: The bill would remove the federal tax deduction for each employee's pay above $1 million, raising tax bills for large public companies and their top earners. Their interest in keeping the deduction runs against ordinary taxpayers, who otherwise share the cost of it.
